description: The 13 curated debate motions of CTO_NOTES_04 §5, each with a hand-written case file for both sides (the board argues the side the user does not pick). Arguments are qualitative: no statistics or numbers. Only motions 5 and 6 list card_topics (the existing tourism and internal_security cards, SYNTHETIC TEST CARDS until the owner replaces them with real, sourced cards; data/cards/README.md). No argument links a card (card_ids removed by ruling 29): the owner must confirm that each real card supports the argument it is attached to before any link is added back. Arguments are listed strongest first. Keywords are for the offline fake listener and the restate check only.
reviewed: Written by the debate builder on Oct 29, 2026; the orchestrator reviewed the 13 motion texts in ruling 21. The case files themselves await the owner's review.

motions.text: This House would ban smartphones in schools up to Class 10.
motions.title: Smartphones in schools

for.claim: Phones in class pull attention away from learning.
for.warrant: Notifications and games compete with the teacher, and young students find it hard to regulate themselves.

for.claim: A ban protects younger students from online harms during the school day.
for.warrant: Cyberbullying, unsuitable content and social media pressure follow children into school through their phones.

for.claim: A clear rule is easier to enforce than case-by-case judgement.
for.warrant: Teachers spend less time policing use when everyone knows phones stay in lockers.

for.claim: School becomes a space for face-to-face friendships.
for.warrant: Breaks without screens push children to talk, play and settle disagreements in person.

against.claim: Phones are learning tools when used well.
against.warrant: Dictionaries, educational videos and practice apps can support lessons, especially where libraries are thin.

against.claim: Parents need to reach children for safety and logistics.
against.warrant: Long commutes and working parents make contact during the day reassuring for families.

against.claim: Teaching responsible use beats banning it.
against.warrant: Students will use phones anyway after school, so guided practice builds the self-control a ban never teaches.

against.claim: A blanket ban hits the students who rely on phones most.
against.warrant: For some families the phone is the only device for homework and school notices, so one rule for all ignores unequal access.

motions.text: This House would replace board exams with continuous assessment.
motions.title: Board exams vs continuous assessment

for.claim: One high-stakes exam measures a single day, not a year of learning.
for.warrant: Illness, anxiety or a bad morning can outweigh months of steady work.

for.claim: Continuous assessment rewards understanding over rote memorisation.
for.warrant: Projects, presentations and regular tests check whether students can apply ideas, not just recall them.

for.claim: Regular feedback helps students improve while there is still time.
for.warrant: A teacher who sees a weak area in the middle of the year can respond, whereas an exam result arrives too late.

against.claim: Board exams set the same paper for everyone, so results are fairer to compare.
against.warrant: Continuous assessment depends on each school and teacher, and marking standards can vary widely.

against.claim: Teacher-marked assessment opens the door to favouritism and pressure.
against.warrant: When the class teacher controls the marks, tuition links, parent pressure or bias can creep in.

against.claim: Continuous assessment can mean continuous stress.
against.warrant: If every week counts, students may never get a break from being graded.

against.claim: Many schools may lack the capacity to run it well.
against.warrant: Good continuous assessment needs trained teachers and time, and overstretched schools may turn it into paperwork.

motions.text: This House would make coding compulsory from Class 6.
motions.title: Compulsory coding

for.claim: Coding teaches logical, step-by-step problem solving.
for.warrant: Breaking a task into instructions trains a way of thinking that helps in maths, science and daily life.

for.claim: Early exposure widens who sees technology careers as possible.
for.warrant: If every child tries coding, interest is not limited to those whose families already know the field.

for.claim: Digital literacy is becoming a basic skill, like reading a map.
for.warrant: Understanding how software works helps citizens use, and question, the technology around them.

against.claim: Many schools lack computers, power or trained teachers.
against.warrant: A compulsory subject without infrastructure becomes rote theory, or widens the gap between schools.

against.claim: The timetable is already full.
against.warrant: Making coding compulsory means cutting time from languages, arts, sport or core subjects.

against.claim: Every child needs strong basics first, not necessarily code.
against.warrant: Reading, arithmetic and reasoning come first, and coding can stay an option for those who are interested.

motions.text: This House believes AI tutors will do Indian students more good than harm.
motions.title: AI tutors

for.claim: AI tutors give patient, one-to-one help at any hour.
for.warrant: A student stuck at night can ask the same question again and again without embarrassment.

for.claim: They can reach students who cannot afford private tuition.
for.warrant: A low-cost tutor on a shared phone can narrow gaps that coaching fees widen.

for.claim: They can teach in a student's own language and at their own pace.
for.warrant: Explanations can be adapted to the learner instead of one pace for a whole class.

against.claim: AI tutors can be confidently wrong.
against.warrant: A student may not notice a fluent but incorrect explanation, and learn the mistake.

against.claim: Easy answers can replace real effort.
against.warrant: If the tutor does the thinking, students may skip the struggle that builds understanding.

against.claim: Teachers do more than explain content.
against.warrant: Mentoring, motivation and noticing a child in trouble need a human relationship.

against.claim: Children's data and privacy are at risk.
against.warrant: Learning platforms collect detailed records about children, and safeguards may lag behind.

motions.text: This House believes tourism does more good than harm to India's hill towns.
motions.title: Tourism in hill towns

for.claim: Tourism brings income to places with few other industries.
for.warrant: Hotels, guides, taxis and shops give local families earnings they might otherwise have to migrate to find.

for.claim: Visitors create demand that pays for better services.
for.warrant: Roads, connectivity and health facilities tend to improve where there is a steady flow of visitors.

for.claim: Tourism gives local culture a market and a reason to survive.
for.warrant: Crafts, food and festivals find buyers, which encourages young people to keep traditions alive.

against.claim: Crowds strain water, waste systems and fragile slopes.
against.warrant: Hill towns have limited carrying capacity, and peak-season pressure can outrun what the land can bear.

against.claim: Much of the money leaves the town.
against.warrant: Outside hotel chains and operators can capture the profits while locals get seasonal, low-paid work.

against.claim: Unplanned construction changes towns for the worse.
against.warrant: Hotels built to meet demand can crowd out residents, raise rents and weaken building safety rules.

against.claim: Residents' daily life suffers in peak season.
against.warrant: Traffic jams and rising prices make ordinary needs harder for people who live there all year.

motions.text: This House believes community policing beats building more police stations.
motions.title: Community policing

for.claim: Trust brings information that buildings cannot.
for.warrant: When residents know and trust officers, they report problems early and help solve cases.

for.claim: Prevention is better than response.
for.warrant: Officers who know a neighbourhood can spot and calm tensions before they turn into crimes.

for.claim: People, not walls, do the policing.
for.warrant: Money spent on staff, training and patrols reaches citizens directly, while a new building still needs officers.

against.claim: Some areas are simply too far from any station.
against.warrant: Where the nearest station is hours away, a complaint or an emergency response depends on physical presence.

against.claim: Community policing needs a base to work from.
against.warrant: Officers need a place for records, custody and coordination, so stations and community work go together.

against.claim: Community policing can be uneven and depend on individuals.
against.warrant: It relies on particular officers and can fade when they are transferred, while a station is a lasting commitment.

motions.text: This House would build metro lines before flyovers in growing cities.
motions.title: Metros before flyovers

for.claim: A metro moves far more people in the same space.
for.warrant: Roads fill up again as cities grow, while rail carries crowds without widening streets.

for.claim: Flyovers can invite more cars and more jams.
for.warrant: When driving gets easier, more people drive, and the congestion returns at the next junction.

for.claim: Public transport is cleaner and fairer.
for.warrant: It cuts pollution and serves people who cannot afford a car.

against.claim: Metros take many years and large budgets to build.
against.warrant: Flyovers can relieve the worst junctions much sooner, while a metro is still under construction.

against.claim: A metro does not reach every doorstep.
against.warrant: Without buses and last-mile links, many trips still need roads, so road fixes remain necessary.

against.claim: Buses, goods and ambulances also need road space.
against.warrant: Freight, emergency vehicles and buses all run on roads, so fixing bottlenecks helps everyone, not just cars.

motions.text: This House would ban single-use plastic completely, even if prices rise.
motions.title: Single-use plastic ban

for.claim: Single-use plastic outlives its use by generations.
for.warrant: It clogs drains, harms animals and breaks into fragments that stay in soil and water.

for.claim: Partial bans leak; a complete ban is clearer.
for.warrant: When some items are allowed, enforcement gets confusing and banned items slip back in.

for.claim: Higher prices push innovation in alternatives.
for.warrant: A firm rule gives businesses a reason to invest in reusable and compostable options.

against.claim: Price rises hurt the poorest most.
against.warrant: Small vendors and low-income buyers feel every extra rupee spent on packaging.

against.claim: Some uses of plastic protect health and reduce waste.
against.warrant: Medical supplies and food packaging can keep things sterile and stop food from spoiling.

against.claim: Collection and recycling may work better than a ban.
against.warrant: The harm comes from plastic that escapes, and better waste systems tackle that without removing useful materials.

motions.text: This House believes work-from-home is better than office work for young professionals.
motions.title: Work from home

for.claim: No commute means more time and energy.
for.warrant: Hours lost in traffic can go to rest, learning or family instead.

for.claim: Remote work opens good jobs beyond big cities.
for.warrant: Young people from smaller towns can work for strong employers without moving away from home.

for.claim: Many people focus better without office interruptions.
for.warrant: Quiet time at home can suit deep work better than a noisy open office.

against.claim: Young professionals learn by watching and asking.
against.warrant: Mentoring and informal advice happen easily side by side and are hard to replicate on calls.

against.claim: Home is not a workplace for everyone.
against.warrant: Shared rooms, unreliable internet and family demands make focus hard for many young people.

against.claim: Being seen and building networks shapes careers.
against.warrant: People who are present build relationships that lead to projects and promotions.

against.claim: The line between work and rest can vanish.
against.warrant: Without leaving for an office, some people work late and struggle to switch off.

motions.text: This House would take a gap year before college.
motions.title: Gap year

for.claim: A gap year helps students choose a course with clarity.
for.warrant: Time to work, volunteer or explore can reveal interests before an expensive choice.

for.claim: Real-world experience builds maturity.
for.warrant: Managing money, work or travel teaches an independence that classrooms rarely do.

for.claim: A break can prevent burnout after school exams.
for.warrant: Students who arrive rested may engage better than those rushing from one exam to the next.

against.claim: Momentum is easy to lose.
against.warrant: Study habits fade, and some students find it hard to return after a year away.

against.claim: A good gap year needs money and safety nets.
against.warrant: Travel and unpaid work are easier for families who can afford them, so the benefit is unequal.

against.claim: Peers move ahead.
against.warrant: Starting later can mean entering jobs later, and some families and employers still question the gap.

motions.text: This House believes cricket gets too much attention compared with other sports in India.
motions.title: Cricket and other sports

for.claim: Sponsorship and coverage follow cricket, leaving other sports short.
for.warrant: Athletes in other sports often struggle for coaching, equipment and visibility.

for.claim: Talent is lost when children see only one path.
for.warrant: A child suited to athletics or football may never try it if cricket is the only dream on offer.

for.claim: A broader sporting culture is healthier for the country.
for.warrant: More sports mean more ways for more people to stay active.

against.claim: Attention follows what fans love.
against.warrant: Cricket's popularity reflects genuine interest, and audiences cannot be ordered to care.

against.claim: Cricket's success can lift other sports.
against.warrant: Leagues, broadcasting and sponsorship models built for cricket show other sports a way to grow.

against.claim: The real gap is grassroots facilities, not attention.
against.warrant: Other sports need playgrounds, coaches and school programmes more than they need less cricket.

motions.text: This House believes filter coffee beats masala chai.
motions.title: Filter coffee vs masala chai

for.claim: Filter coffee is a craft.
for.warrant: The decoction, the frothy pour between tumbler and dabarah, and the timing make every cup a small ritual.

for.claim: Its flavour is bold and clear.
for.warrant: Coffee's roasted depth stands on its own instead of hiding behind spices.

for.claim: It wakes you up properly.
for.warrant: A strong cup gives a firm start to a morning or a long study session.

against.claim: Masala chai is made in almost every home and on every street corner.
against.warrant: Its reach makes it a shared ritual across regions and seasons.

against.claim: Chai can be tuned to every mood.
against.warrant: Ginger, cardamom, cloves or tulsi let each cup change with the weather and the person.

against.claim: Chai is about company.
against.warrant: The chai break is where conversations, friendships and ideas happen.

motions.text: This House believes street food is India's greatest culinary treasure.
motions.title: Street food

for.claim: Street food brings regional variety to a single city block.
for.warrant: From chaat to vada pav to momos, flavours from many regions show up where everyone can taste them.

for.claim: It is affordable for everyone.
for.warrant: A student, a worker and a visitor can all eat well at the same stall.

for.claim: It keeps family recipes and skills alive.
for.warrant: Many stalls pass their techniques down through generations of cooks.

against.claim: Home cooking holds the deepest traditions.
against.warrant: Festival dishes and everyday family food carry knowledge that rarely reaches a street stall.

against.claim: Hygiene varies widely.
against.warrant: Without clean water and safe storage, a treasure can become a health risk.

against.claim: Calling one style the greatest ignores the rest.
against.warrant: Community kitchens, regional thalis and home kitchens are treasures too: different, not lesser.
